questions.question: How does specificity actually compute — and how do modern tools (layers, :where, !important) manage it?
questions.title: Specificity Order
questions.direct_answer: Specificity is a three-column score (inline styles > IDs > classes/attributes/pseudo-classes > elements/pseudo-elements), compared LEFT to RIGHT: (1,0,0) beats (0,10,0) — ten classes lose to one ID. Ties break by ORDER (later rule wins). The override ladder in modern CSS: @layer — rules in LATER-declared (or explicitly ordered) layers WIN over earlier ones, and UNLAYERED styles beat ALL layered ones (the import order: @layer reset, base, components, utilities — utilities win by layer position with LOW specificity inside); :where() drops its argument's specificity to 0 (styles that can ALWAYS be overridden — the reset/normalize pattern); :is() KEEPS the highest specificity of its arguments (the old trap: :is(#a, .b) inherits ID-level specificity); !important flips the whole contest — the last resort that cascades into specificity wars.

sections.title: Interview Answer
Mental Model
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TD
    C[cascade order] --> O1[origin + importance]
    O1 --> O2[unlayered beats layered, then @layer order]
    O2 --> O3[specificity: inline id class element]
    O3 --> O4[source order breaks ties]
    SP[id beats any class count] --> BIG[(0,1,0,0) > (0,0,n,n)]
    LAYER[@layer utilities declared last] --> WIN[utilities win — managed override]
    WHERE[:where()] --> ZERO[specificity 0 — the overridable reset]
    IS[:is a b] --> KEEP[max specificity of args — the trap]
    IMP[!important] --> LAST[last resort — one-way door]
```

sections.title: Deep Dive
sections.content:
Why specificity tuples, not numbers (the design insight): the columns exist so that QUANTITY can never defeat KIND at a higher tier — you cannot out-class an ID with a thousand classes; that property is what makes the cascade predictable and also what makes an ID in a stylesheet a permanence decision (the industry norm: avoid IDs in selectors precisely because they're un-overridable by class-based systems).

The inline-vs-!important boundary cases interviewers probe: inline styles sit ABOVE all author rules (specificity 1,0,0,0-ish in the tuple) — the reason JS style writes beat stylesheets and why CSS custom properties set inline (el.style.setProperty('--x', v)) are the sanctioned JS-influence channel; and transitions get temporarily applied AS they run (the spec places transitioning values at a special cascade origin — which is why a transitioning property can beat a same-specificity rule during the animation, a real 'why did that style apply mid-transition' answer).

The systems-level payoff (why @layer is the headline change): before layers, every large codebase converged on either specificity inflation (BEM's flat .block__element classes, all (0,0,1,0) — order-dependent) or import-order discipline (fragile). @layer makes the PRIORITY an explicit, greppable declaration at the top of the file: resets can't bleed, third-party CSS can be slotted BELOW yours (unlayered beats layered — your overrides need no specificity tricks), and utility systems sit at the top by declaration, not by escalating selectors. Combined with :where() for zero-specificity defaults, the modern answer to 'how do you keep CSS maintainable at scale' is layers + flat selectors — not !important.
